body.text: These Australians are rewriting the Australian Dream – in Berlin
These three millennials struggled to achieve the Australian Dream. This is what happened when they moved to Berlin.

In the buzzing, pub-lined streets of Berlin's Neukölln, Toby Knyvett is rarely able to walk far without stopping. The Australian lighting designer, recognisable by his rock-star hair and broad Sydney accent, has just finished a library reading session with his two-year-old son Adam. Groceries are tucked beneath the child's stroller. But before heading home to cook dinner, Toby is taking Adam to a nearby playground to catch the last of the afternoon sunshine.

During the 15-minute walk he stops every few steps to greet someone: a tattoo artist, the owner of a record shop, a customer emerging from a Späti, one of Berlin's ubiquitous corner shops. Friends crouch down to play with Adam while Toby exchanges neighbourhood news. These small encounters are among his favourite parts of the day.

At the playground, Adam clambers over the equipment with a cheerful grin. Toby recognises several parents through his son. There are around 11 playgrounds within walking distance of the family's tiny apartment, along with Adam's daycare, shops, a library, music venues and several major public-transport lines.

It is a compact life that Toby struggled to imagine achieving in Sydney. Adam was born in Berlin to Australian parents. His mother also works in the city's creative sector. Toby grew up on the outskirts of Sydney.
In 2016, as he approached 30, Toby began looking closely at his future in Australia.
His profile as a freelance lighting designer was rising. He was securing work at the Sydney Opera House and designing large installations, but the economics still did not add up.
Even if he became one of Australia's 10 leading lighting designers, Toby calculated, he would be "lucky to ever get a mortgage on a house less than a 90-minute drive from the city".
"I grew up on the fringes of Sydney, and I was sick of book-ending every long day with more hours of driving," he said.

Toby had always wanted to live overseas and was approaching the age limit for several working-holiday visas. Following his partner to Berlin, Toby initially planned to spend three months in Germany before trying Canada and the United Kingdom.
"But I never left," he said. "Berlin just clicked straight away."

As the cost of living climbs in Australia, for many taking with it the dream of home ownership, some like Toby are exploring what it might be like to live and work in a different country. But how significant are the potential savings or career boost? And how does a cheaper way of life or greater work opportunities stack up against leaving behind family and homeland?
A career not possible in Australia
What initially attracted Toby was Berlin's less commercial and more collective cultural scene.
"In Sydney, you have to be a multimillionaire to have a pub and put on some bands, while in Berlin it's often done by collectives of volunteers," he said, exaggerating a little to make his point.
Berlin was not free from bureaucracy, he cautioned, but it offered relatively affordable housing, a lower cost of living and public transport that made living without a car possible.

Establishing himself professionally still took time. It was around 10 months before Toby secured his first locally paid job. Limited German language prevented him from working in text-heavy theatre, pushing him instead towards music, software and clients elsewhere in Europe.
Then, in 2018, an unexpected opportunity transformed his career.

Volkswagen offered Toby a full-time position using the same interactive software he had employed in his lighting installations to help develop prototype vehicles. He initially planned to stay for a year or two, but remained for six.
"When Volkswagen came along, that was something I could never have done in Australia," he said. "We just don't make much stuff like that in Australia anymore, let alone design it."

Today, Germany's contracting automotive industry has made employment less secure. Toby is combining his manufacturing experience with his creative skills to develop his own software and electronic products.
Berlin did not eliminate career uncertainty. It gave him a different range of possibilities.
After six years of full-time work at Volkswagen, Toby secured permanent residency in Germany, having previously lived and worked there on an EU Blue Card.

A secure contract with Volkswagen also allowed Toby to do something he believed might never be possible in Sydney: buy a home. In 2019, he purchased a 50-square-metre apartment in Berlin. His initial mortgage repayments were approximately €1,000 (about $1,580) a month, although he has temporarily reduced them while establishing his business.

Like many Australians, Toby grew up believing that the Australian Dream involved owning a detached house. "I didn't foresee that being an apartment," he said. "But, on the other hand, I never really enjoyed mowing the lawn."
'Hacking' the Australian Dream

Professor Alan Gamlen, director of the Australian National University's Migration Hub, said the phrase "Australian Dream" was less firmly embedded in the national culture than its American counterpart.

While the American Dream emphasised individualism and self-made success, Australia had traditionally placed greater value on egalitarianism and what was more commonly described as the "Australian way of life", he said.
Nevertheless, home ownership remained central to that ideal.
"The quarter-acre paradise — the ability to buy a home and be better off than your parents were — that's part of it," Gamlen said.

Toby believes German property prices are somewhat lower, but says the financing and urban infrastructure make the greater difference. When he bought, he was able to fix his mortgage interest rate for 10 years, allowing the family to plan around a predictable repayment.
Dense German cities also make more homes practical places to live, he said. His family can reach shops, childcare, playgrounds, cultural venues and public transport without owning a car.
"There was no way I was ever going to get that utility in an affordable home in Sydney," he said.
The deposit that had never been sufficient for a house on Sydney's fringe covered 40 per cent of his inner-city Berlin apartment.

Toby bought his apartment for less than €300,000 ($486, 267) and expects to pay off the mortgage over 10 years. German home loans commonly have fixed monthly repayments, with interest rates locked in for 10, 15 or even 20 years, giving borrowers long-term certainty.

Unlike in Australia, where offset accounts use savings to reduce the balance on which interest is charged, German borrowers are more likely to negotiate Sondertilgungen — the right to make additional repayments each year.

"Another detail is that there are transfer taxes and fees, plus many apartments come with absolutely no fixtures, so you may need to immediately buy a full kitchen and bathroom," Toby said. "The bank loan doesn't cover this so it comes from your deposit side. [The outlay] might be 12-15 per cent of the entire apartment cost."

By comparison, $420,000 in Toby's hometown could buy a studio apartment in North Sydney of about 37 square metres including a balcony. For $450,000 he could afford a two bedroom, two bathroom plus car space apartment with its own private balcony. The catch? It would be 30 kilometres from the CBD.
"I feel like I kind of hacked the Australian Dream," he said of his Berlin life. "I got out of the Sydney rat race by splicing some Berlin in."

Berlin's housing market is not a utopia, however. Strong tenant protections allow many residents to remain in their homes over the long term, but newcomers face a severe shortage of available apartments and high-priced temporary sublets.
Toby advises new arrivals to prepare for a year or more of moving between temporary homes before securing a permanent lease.
The cost of raising a family far from home
For Toby, the greatest costs of living overseas cannot be measured through rent or mortgage payments.
Warning: the following section discusses the loss of a child.
Toby and his Aussie partner had their first daughter in 2022. She was born with a rare genetic illness and died when she was eight months old.
"We miss her every damn day," he said.

Living far from their families made an already devastating experience even more difficult. Toby and his partner were grateful that their parents were able to visit their daughter before she died. Yet the experience made him acutely aware of the downsides of raising children on the other side of the world. A family trip to Australia can cost more than €3,000 (about $4,740), making frequent visits difficult.

After struggling to find an English-language support community that met his needs, Toby founded Child Loss Berlin on May 12, 2025 — the anniversary of his daughter's death. Through the group, he supports other English-speaking parents in Berlin who have lost children.
Toby and his partner's second child, Adam, was born in 2024. Toby now divides his time between parenting, building his business and supporting other bereaved families.

Berlin's childcare system has helped make this possible. Publicly funded daycare is free, with parents normally contributing €23 (about $36) a month towards lunch, although centres can charge for optional extras. Toby's family pays approximately €43 a month (about $68).
The financial contrast with Australia is considerable. But Toby's experience also shows affordable childcare cannot fully replace grandparents or the wider family network left behind.
For now, his version of the Australian Dream remains rooted in Berlin, but its future is uncertain.

Even if he eventually sells his Berlin apartment, Toby worries it would provide only a modest deposit for a suitable Sydney property. After nine years outside Australia, he has also missed years of superannuation contributions."I think everyone has to find their own way to hack the Australian Dream now," he said.
Berlin gave Duckie L'Orange an audience

Wearing little more than dazzling earrings and an elaborate headdress, Australian cabaret performer Duckie L'Orange sashayed onto the stage in Berlin's iconic cultural centre ufaFabrik with a playful mixture of flirtation and humour. Beneath the spotlight, her vivid facial expressions and exaggerated movements captivated the crowd.

Duckie's comedy is physical, absurd and deliberately confronting. In her best-known repertoire, Bumdog, she appears as a naked dog — a performance that first found a small following in Sydney's underground cabaret scene but reached a dramatically larger audience after she moved to Germany.
In Berlin and elsewhere in Germany, the act has taken her to theatres, festivals, a tour of more than 10 cities and national television as a contestant on Germany's Got Talent.

The success challenges the familiar image of Berlin as an isolated playground for experimental artists. Duckie, 40, has performed the routine not only in the capital's alternative venues, but in ordinary German towns and even at family-friendly festivals.
"Maybe producers are more prepared to take a risk," she said.

Duckie believes Germany's less anxious relationship with nudity is important. She points to the country's tradition of Freikörperkultur — free-body culture — in which naked swimming, lakeside bathing and mixed saunas are not automatically treated as sexual or shameful.
Starting with no network

Like Toby, Duckie has spent about a decade in Berlin, moving from Sydney in 2017. She had long felt geographically removed from the places where major cultural activity seemed to be happening, an issue raised by many Australians.

Moving to Melbourne was one possibility, but it would still have required Duckie to find housing, employment and an entirely new professional network. If she was going to make that effort, she decided, she might as well go somewhere completely different.
Berlin offered an extensive cultural scene, relatively affordable living costs and easier access to the rest of Europe.

She arrived knowing nobody and without a job, but began securing performances almost immediately. Within her first few months, Duckie was booked for small tours — an opportunity that had never arisen in Australia.
Although Sydney had excellent cabaret performers, she said, the market was small, venues were limited and travelling to performances was often inconvenient and expensive.

Germany offered a different scale: a population of more than 80 million in a country smaller than New South Wales, with theatres in towns across the country and neighbouring European markets within easy reach.

"There are more audiences, more venues and more performances," Duckie said. "It's easier for everybody to go to see performances because they live close by, because the transport is great and because it's not too expensive."

That accessibility creates room not only for established artists, she added, but for beginners and performers experimenting with new work. "In Sydney, there are really great performers. But beginner performers who might become great have a difficult time. There is not enough space for people to actually experiment, which could lead to innovation," Duckie said.

Duckie is particularly proud of the clown show she founded in 2019, called Clown Slam. Through it, she met other performers, discovered venues and developed collaborative work with artists from Germany and other countries.
Berlin's international population has made the performance scene more diverse, she said, while working with German artists has also helped her understand the country's national theatre network.
With the growth of her German language skills, from time-to-time she now performs in German.
An artistic career still requires hustle
Yet opportunities do not guarantee a stable income.

Duckie's performances might be unpaid, particularly when they form part of a fundraiser, or they might earn as much as €350 (about $550) — the recommended industry rate — or even more. During busy periods, Duckie can perform several times a week, but at other times she focuses on different projects.

The reality is that even in Berlin's thriving creative scene Duckie cannot support herself through performing alone. To make a living, she also produces shows, helps artistic directors develop strategies and funding applications, designs cultural projects and assists in delivering them.
"The main thing is that it's less expensive to live here," she said. "But, in my opinion, it's around the same level of hustle that you would have to do anywhere in Australia. It's not easy."

Berlin has also become substantially more expensive since she arrived almost a decade ago. Duckie estimates some food prices have risen by more than 50 per cent, while coffee and the prices offered to many newcomers seeking apartments have almost doubled.

At current prices, let us say, a 70-square-metre, two-bedroom flat in Neukölln — a gritty, multicultural and creative neighbourhood — costs around €1,000 ($1,608) a month before heating and utilities — called "Kaltmiete" in German. Compare that with a median $700 a week for a two-bedroom unit in a suburb like Marrickville, in Sydney's inner-west, which has a similar feel to Neukölln.

However, as Toby also pointed out, Berlin is famous for being difficult to find apartment. Newcomers relying on current listings — particularly furnished apartments — may need to pay €1,300–€2,000 ($2,090-$3,216) per month before utilities in wealthier and more established suburbs such as Schöneberg or Charlottenburg. Expats also typically face higher rent because they may experience discrimination or miss out on rent-control laws that cap long-term rents.
As a result many newcomers live out of their suitcase, moving from place-to-place for months before finding a permanent and affordable place to live.

When Duckie first arrived, she was unable to secure a permanent home for two years. Long-term tenants with older, inexpensive contracts were reluctant to surrender them, while newcomers competed for a shrinking number of available properties.

Freestanding homes are more common on Berlin's outskirts and sell for an average of around €3,830 ($6,203) per square metre. But in Berlin apartment living dominates: 87 per cent of the city's dwellings are in multi-unit buildings.

Everyday costs include roughly €1 ($1.61) for a litre of organic whole milk or €4 ($6.43) for a standard two-hour public transport ticket, a different way of charging for transport that makes comparison with large Australian cities difficult. Daily commuters pay €63 ($101) for a monthly, unlimited Deutschland Ticket for urban travel. This ticket allows travel around Germany by regional train, if you have time to spend on the many transfers and slow travel.
But the financial calculation is only part of the story.
The ANU's Professor Gamlen said living overseas had long functioned as a rite of passage for young Australians, shaped partly by the country's colonial relationship with Britain and Europe.
What was once primarily "a voyage of self-discovery" had increasingly become a concentrated period of building cultural and professional capital, he said.
Australians might explain their departure through housing costs, wages or working conditions, but those rational calculations existed alongside a deeper cultural expectation.
"Young Australians have always travelled, and there's an expectation that they will travel and live in Europe or North America for a while," Gamlen said.

For some careers, international experience could also act as a professional credential, helping Australians demonstrate that they had worked beyond what could feel like a relatively small domestic market.
For Duckie, the traditional Australian Dream — a house, garden and car space — belongs largely to her parents' generation.

"I think the Australian Dream is bullshit," she said. "Our parents' generation had this dream and achieved this dream. But we can't do it anymore without working ourselves to the bone all the time for the rest of our lives."
She misses her family and the Australian landscape, and she would not rule out returning. But doing so would require sacrifices.
"I would be happy to go back," she said, "but it would be a compromise in many ways."
'The biggest gamble'
While Toby and Duckie built their versions of the Australian Dream in Berlin, Broden Tadros eventually brought his overseas experience home.

Broden moved to Berlin in 2017 at the age of 24, following his partner Jessi after they had been together for just over a year. The couple embarked on what he describes as a "one-way trip", travelling through India and Sri Lanka before arriving in Germany.
"It was the biggest gamble of our lives," he said.

With little sales experience and no German, Broden found a job with a company organising English-language conferences across Germany. Two Australians interviewed him and offered him the position, where he earned €30,000 (about $47,400) a year plus commission.

The salary was lower than Broden might have earned in Australia, but Berlin's cheaper rent, groceries, alcohol and social life gave the couple more freedom. They paid €840 a month for their apartment ($1,372), split between them, and used much of their remaining income to travel around Europe.
More importantly, the job gave Broden international sales experience that later helped him move into marketing and business growth.
"Having that cultural awareness and sensitivity has been incredibly valuable in my career," he said.

Berlin also tested and strengthened the young couple's relationship. Broden describes himself as outgoing and his partner — now his wife — as more grounded. Their differences, he said, made them a strong travelling partnership.
A ruby they found in Jaipur was later set into Jessi's engagement ring, a lasting reminder of the journey that carried them to Berlin.

After just over a year in Germany, however, family considerations began pulling them back to Australia. Both wanted to be present for their parents as they grew older. He initially wanted to remain in Berlin for another year, but now feels grateful that they returned when they did. Broden returned in early 2019, a year before the pandemic closed borders and made international travel far more difficult.
Today, aged 34, Broden and his wife own an apartment in Sydney's inner-west.
Broden acknowledges that they were fortunate: after returning from Berlin, his first job was with Westpac, and employee benefits helped make their purchase possible.

Even so, he considers the traditional Australian Dream of home ownership increasingly out of reach for many people. Their apartment rose approximately $300,000 in value over four years before falling back slightly — an increase that illustrates how quickly Sydney property prices can move beyond the reach of those who have not already entered the market.
Broden's priorities have also changed since becoming a father.
The couple pays $560 a fortnight for three days of childcare each week —approximately $1,210 a month or $14,560 a year. The contrast with Toby's experience in Berlin is stark.

For Toby, the low cost of childcare helps make it possible to raise a family while establishing a new business. Yet for Broden, childcare represents another substantial expense layered on top of Sydney's housing and everyday living costs.

Despite increased childcare subsidies, rent assistance and moves to strengthen tenants' rights, Australia's affordability crisis has deepened over the past decade, with housing prices rising much faster than household incomes and younger Australians facing growing barriers to home ownership.

While the cost of living in Berlin is rising, most assessments continue to place it as more affordable than Australian cities such as Sydney, where Broden now lives. Berlin is also cheaper than cities such as Hobart, Perth, Darwin and Melbourne but more closely aligned with Adelaide and Brisbane.
However affordability is not the only consideration when deciding where to build a life.

Broden misses his Berlin friends and remembers his year in Germany as one of the happiest and most formative periods of his life. But he is no longer the 24-year-old who arrived there with a partner, a suitcase and uncertain plans.
"I feel like a completely different person from who I was back in those days," he said. "They are still some of my fondest memories."
Now a father with a career and a home in Sydney, he does not imagine moving back to Berlin. He found opportunity abroad, but ultimately chose to build his life closer to home.
Berlin nevertheless remains part of the life he and his wife created together — in his international career, in the friendships they still maintain, and in the Jaipur ruby she wears on her finger.
An emotional calculation
For Australians weighing whether to leave in search of a more affordable life, the experiences of Toby, Duckie and Broden offer no simple answer.

For now, Duckie L'Orange is happy to remain in Berlin. The main development that could persuade her to leave would be a significant change in Germany's political climate — particularly policies that made the country more hostile towards immigrants.
"I'm very happy with my life here right now," she said. "If there are changes in government that become very anti-immigration, that would be a reason for me to leave."

Returning to Australia would not be unwelcome, but it would require compromises: higher housing and everyday costs, and a much smaller market for the experimental performance work she has developed in Europe.
About one million Australian citizens live overseas at any one time, with about 430,000 Australian-born migrants revealed in UN migrant data as long-term residents of foreign countries.

However these figures do not show how many moved for a cheaper way of life compared with moving for jobs, travel or family, for example. The Australian Bureau of Statistics also does not record cost of living as a reason for leaving Australia.
Housing strongly influenced where Australians moved within the country, Gamlen said, but international migration involved a more complicated calculation.
Moving abroad could offer cheaper housing or a different lifestyle, but it also brought visa requirements, language barriers, disrupted careers and the loss of family and professional networks.

Toby, however, is already considering a journey in the opposite direction. Although Berlin made home ownership, affordable childcare and an unexpected career possible, the pull of family is becoming stronger as his parents grow older and he wants his son to spend more time with them.
"I'm already starting to put one foot back in Australia," he said.

Berlin can provide cheaper housing, heavily subsidised childcare, accessible public transport and a larger cultural market. It can also mean lower salaries, difficult bureaucracy, lost superannuation and years spent far from family.
Gamlen cautioned against interpreting these individual departures as evidence of a wider Australian exodus.

"Australia, as an economy and as a destination, is still very appealing internationally," he said. "The strength of the economy, the strength of the Australian dollar, the standard of living and the quality of life are all very high by global standards."

He said there had been no unusually large increase in Australians choosing to leave, but rather a "steady trickle" that fluctuated with economic conditions and reflected a long cultural tradition of overseas travel.

For Australians motivated primarily by affordability, Europe was not necessarily the obvious solution. The Australian dollar stretched further in parts of south-east Asia, he said, contributing to the growth of digital nomadism, retirement migration and people dividing their lives between countries.
Moving overseas may allow some Australians to construct a different life, but it is not a universal answer to the country's cost-of-living crisis.
Moving overseas may not deliver a new Australian Dream. But it can change what that dream looks like — and where people ultimately choose to pursue it.
